Introduction
[1] Milton McClelland (Mr McClelland) is a registered nurse.
[2] Mr McClelland faces three charges (the Charges) pursuant to s 100(1)(c) of the Health
Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 (the Act) in that he has been convicted of
one or more offences that reflect adversely on his fitness to practise as a nurse.
[3] The Charges relate to 10 convictions entered on 24 January 2019 in the Palmerston North
District Court. These convictions are: firstly, five convictions for exportation of
objectionable publications pursuant to s 56 of the Customs and Excise Act 1996;
secondly, four convictions for possession of objectionable material pursuant to
s 131(A)(1) of the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act 1993; and thirdly,
one conviction for the making of an objectionable publication pursuant to s 124(1) of the
Films, Videos and Publications Classifications Act 1993.
[4] Mr McClelland had pleaded guilty to each of these representative Charges. He was
convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for 10 months two weeks.
[5] On 19 August 2019 the Professional Conduct Committee (PCC) appointed by the Nursing
Council of New Zealand (the Nursing Council) laid the three disciplinary charges in the
Tribunal. The particulars of the Charges are set out in the Schedule to this decision.1
[6] The PCC alleges that these convictions separately and cumulatively reflect adversely on
Mr McClelland’s fitness to practise pursuant to s 100(1)(c) of the Act.
The hearing
[7] Mr McClelland did not attend the hearing and he was not represented by counsel. Mr
McClelland advised the Executive Officer of the Tribunal on 30 August 2019 that he did
not wish to attend the hearing.
[8] At no stage of the proceedings was there an application for non-publication orders by Mr
McClelland and none were made.
[9] The hearing was heard in Wellington on 25 November 2019. The hearing proceeded by
way of written and oral submissions from counsel for the PCC.
1 Amendments were made to typos in the orginal Charges laid at the commencement of the hearing and the
corrected Charges and particulars are set out in the Schedule to this decision.

4
Evidence
[10] The PCC provided a bundle of documents which included the Certified Copy of the Entry
of the Criminal Record (Court Record)2 and the Summary of Facts prepared by the New
Zealand Customs service for the criminal prosecution.3 There was no further contextual
or background information to the circumstances of the offending provided to the Tribunal.
The Tribunal was advised by counsel for the PCC that the Nursing Council was unable
to provide the sentencing notes from the District Court hearing.
[11] There was some email communication from Mr McClelland to the Nursing Council of
New Zealand prior to the hearing.4 He also provided a statement of his financial position
dated 22 October 2019.5
Background facts
[12] The following background facts are taken from the New Zealand Customs Service’
Summary of Facts for the criminal prosecution.6
SUMMARY OF FACTS AS AT 08/10/2018
Background
1. In 2018, Google photos identified a New Zealand user exporting objectionable
publications depicting the sexual exploitation of children.
2. The detection was forwarded onto the National Center for Missing and Exploitation
Children ‘NCMEC’ based in the United States of America. When the NCMEC and
Google Photos believe a user is from New Zealand, a report is generated and
forwarded onto New Zealand law enforcement authorities.
3. In August 2018 Customs received the report which contained the following
information relating to the offending user:
• Name: Milt Mcclelland
• Email Address: miltmcclelland@gmail.com
• Secondary Email: miltmcclelland@aol.com
Exportation Offending

4. Analysis of the report identified between 18 April 2018 and 26 June 2018, a Google
Photos account with the name ‘Milt Mcclelland’ uploaded nine objectionable
publications depicting the sexual exploitation of children. The publications were
uploaded to Google Photos, a photo sharing and storage service used by people
internationally to upload their photos and videos to Google’s cloud storage service.
5. Google do not have any servers within New Zealand, they are all based off shore and
the uploading of objectionable publications is defined as exportation.
6. The following is a brief description of an objectionable publication uploaded/exported
to the Google Photos account on 18 April 2018.
File Name: hoqn9E.gif
Description: ‘A female child preforming [sic] fellatio on a male penis’.
7. The report supplied internet protocol numbers for the exportation of the publications
and internet connection history between 18 April 2018 and 26 June 2018.
8. Customs made enquires with New Zealand internet service providers who operated
the internet protocol (IP) numbers to identify the offending user. The results identified
the IP address used to upload of the publication was linked to a hotel at 2 Hall Street,
Dannevirke.
9. Further enquiries with internet service providers identified objectionable publications
were being uploaded from a Spark mobile internet connection.
Search Warrant:
10. On 20 September 2018 a search warrant was executed at 2 Hall Street, Dannevirke,
the defendant was located living at the address and electronic devices were retained.
Questioning At Search Warrant:
11. The defendant was questioned during the search warrant where he made the following
statements to a Customs officer:
• He stated anything involving a person under the age of 16 is illegal and would be
considered objectionable
• He stated all of his electronic devices require either a pin or password which only
he knows
• He lives at 2 Hall Street, Dannevirke and was also living there at the time of the
export offending
• He previously used a Google photos account and recognised the reported
accounts email address
• He visits websites that depict the sexual exploitation of children

6
• He admitted he last viewed objectionable material the day of the warrant
• He has had an interest in this type of material for a number of years
• He knew that the Google photo service is located in America
On conclusion to the search warrant the defendant was arrested by Customs for the
exportation of objectionable publications from New Zealand.
Examination of Electronic Devices:

Possession offending: CRN18054500849

Description: ‘Female child wearing no pants. An adult male inserts his erect penis
into the child’s genitalia.

Registration pursuant to the Child protection (Child Sex Offender Government
Agency Registration) Act 2016 (the Act)
22. This offending discloses an offence or offences listed in Schedule 2 of the Act. On
conviction, if the defendant is sentenced to a term of imprisonment then by operation
of law they will be registered on the Child Sex Offender Register. If the defendant is
to receive a non-custodial sentence then they may be registered at the Court’s
discretion pursuant to section 8 of the Act.
23. The defendant is Milton David Mcclelland, a 65 year old male who has not appeared
before the New Zealand Courts for related charges.
Relevant law under the HPCA Act
[13] The primary purpose of the Tribunal’s disciplinary powers is the protection of the public
by the maintenance of professional standards.7
7 B v Medical Council Noted in [2005] 3 NZLR 810, Elias J at page 15.

8
[14] A further purpose is to maintain the integrity of the profession. In Dentice v The Valuers
Registration Board8 Eichelbaum CJ described professional disciplinary procedures in the
following way:
Although, in respect of different professions, the nature of the unprofessional or incompetent
conduct, which will attract disciplinary charges is variously described, there is a common
thread of scope and purpose. Such provisions exist to enforce a high standard of propriety
and professional conduct; to ensure that no person unfitted because of his or her conduct
should be allowed to practise the profession in question; to protect both the public, and the
profession itself, against persons unfit to practise; and to enable the profession or calling, as
a body, to ensure that the conduct of members conforms to the standards generally expected
of them. See generally, In Re A Medical Practitioner [1959] NZLR 784 at pp 800, 802, 805
and 814.
[15] The purpose of disciplinary proceedings is also the setting of standards.9 There may also
be a punitive element to disciplinary proceedings. As there has been a criminal conviction
the Tribunal may not impose a fine.10
[16] The burden of proving the Charge is on the PCC.
[17] The standard of proof in professional disciplinary cases is the civil standard, namely on
the balance of probabilities, rather than the criminal standard of proof. The gravity of the
allegations is an important factor. The greater the gravity of the allegations, the higher
the standard of proof.11
[18] Orders can be made under s 100(1)(c) of the Act if the Tribunal, after conducting a
hearing on a charge laid, makes the finding that the practitioner has been convicted of a
qualifying offence that reflects adversely on his or her fitness to practise.
Tribunal’s consideration of the Charge
Qualifying convictions
[19] There are two elements of the Charge under s 100(1)(c) of the Act. First, the practitioner
has been convicted of an offence. The second is that the offence reflects adversely on the
practitioner’s fitness to practise.
[20] The first element of the Charge under s 100(1)(c) is established in this case as
Mr McClelland has qualifying convictions as they relate to offences punishable by
8 [1992] 1 NZLR 720, at page 724 line 40.
9 B v Medical Council [2005] 3 NZLR 810, Elias J.
10 HPCA Act, s 101(2).
11 Z v Dental Complaints Assessments Committee [2009] 1 NZLR 1 (SC).

9
imprisonment for a term of three months or longer.12 In summary, the three kinds of
convictions and the corresponding maximum penalty are as follows:
(a) A conviction under ss 56 and 209(1A)(a) of the Customs and Excise Act 1996 is
punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years.
(b) A conviction under s 124(1) of the Films, Videos and Publications Classifications
Act 1993 is punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years.
(c) A conviction under s 131A(1) of the Films, Videos and Publications Classifications
Act 1993 is punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years.
[21] In relation to all three disciplinary Charges (and corresponding convictions) the
Certificate of Conviction is conclusive proof that Mr McClelland has committed these
offences.13
Fitness to practise
[22] The second element is concerned with whether these convictions reflect adversely on
Mr McClelland’s practice as a registered nurse.
[23] “Fitness to practise” is not defined in the Act. The Tribunal accepts that it is now well
established that the test for conduct that reflects adversely on a health practitioner’s fitness
to practise goes far beyond a health practitioner’s clinical and technical competence. The
Tribunal is entitled to take into account circumstances of the offending.14
[24] In Murdoch,15 a physiotherapist who was convicted of dishonestly using documents with
intent to obtain pecuniary advantage from a credit card. In relation to fitness to practise,
the Tribunal stated that:
Fitness to practise cannot, in the context of a conviction, relate only to the practitioner’s
clinical ability. It must also involve a moral consideration and conduct which offends the
law is immoral or unethical, must [reflect] adversely on the practitioner’s fitness to [practise].
Registration carries with it obligation to behave in a way which is ethical, honest in
accordance with the law. Failure to uphold the law or dishonesty must adversely affect a
practitioner’s fitness to practise.
[25] In Beardsmore,16 Mr Beardsmore had been convicted of seven charges of knowingly
making an objectionable publication and one charge of possessing an objectionable
publication. These convictions involved publications of young children engaged in
12 Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003, s 100(2)(b).
13 Evidence Act 2006, s 47.
14 Dunkley (368/Med11/175P) and Martin (45/Nur05/19P).
15 76/Phys06/45P at [34].
16 243/Nur09/117P at [22].

10
sexual activity. The Tribunal referred to other authorities about the nature of these
offences:17
In Department of Internal Affairs v Wigzell (20 November 2007, Clifford J, CRI-2007-485-
110), the Court referred to a statement by the Chairman of the United Kingdom Sentencing
Advisory Panel, Professor Martin Waisick, as follows:
“It is fundamental to our proposal that sentences for these offences should reflect the harm
suffered by children who are abused and exploited by the production and distribution of
indecent photographs. An offender sentenced for possession of child pornography should
be treated as being in some degree complicit in the original abuse which was involved in
the making of the images. Sentences for possession should also reflect the continuing
damage done to the victim or victims, through copying and dissemination of the
pornographic images. Those who make or distribute the images bear a more direct
responsibility for their eventual use, as well as for encouraging further production.”
[26] In Lockett, Mr Lockett had been convicted of 17 charges of knowingly possessing
objectionable images pursuant to s 131A of the Films, Videos and Publications Act 1993.
In determining whether the charge was established, the Tribunal said:18
In the District Court, the Judge referred to the following statement made in another similar
case, by another Judge:
“The sexual abuse of children is abhorrent and the behaviour of those who indulge in such
behaviour is always firmly denounced by the Courts. Those who purchase images of such
abuse provide a market, and so an encouragement of those who carry out the sexual abuse
which is captured in these images. The protection of children from this exploitation is in
my view a paramount consideration today. The denunciation of the conduct is also a very
important factor.”
[27] Counsel for the PCC submitted that the Charges against Mr McClelland constitute a
significant departure from standards reasonably expected of a nurse. The conduct giving
rise to the convictions reflects adversely on his fitness to practise as a registered nurse.
Such conduct falls well below that expected of a nurse and those failures are significant
enough to warrant disciplinary sanction. His conduct must be regarded as totally
unacceptable behaviour for any registered nurse.
[28] The PCC further submitted that it is appropriate that a sanction is imposed on
Mr McClelland to demonstrate to both the public and other members of the profession
that conduct such as Mr McClelland’s convictions for pornography offences are not
considered acceptable by the nursing profession, indeed any health-related profession.
17 PCC v Beardsmore 243/Nur09/117P at [22].
18 246/Nur09/118P at [23].

11
[29] The Tribunal concurs with the PCC’s submission. Not only was Mr McClelland
convicted for exporting and possessing objectionable child pornography, he was also
creating videos by filming from another device, depicting sexual exploitation of a child.
As cited in Beardsmore, by making available images for others to access there was
re-abuse of the victims. There were also a significant number of images involved as these
were representative charges. Mr McClelland knew that he was in breach of these
censorship laws and his offending in relation to child sexual material had been identified
on his computer devices since 2016.
[30] The Tribunal finds that these Charges are established. The convictions separately and
cumulatively reflect adversely on Mr McClelland’s fitness to practise as a registered nurse
pursuant to s 100(1)(c) of the Act. The Tribunal has no hesitation in concluding that
such conduct constitutes a major departure from legal, professional and ethical standards
expected from nurses and are of such a serious nature to warrant disciplinary sanction.
Penalty
Penalty principles
[31] The available penalties under s 101 of the Act are: cancellation of registration; suspension
for a period not exceeding three years; imposition of conditions on practice for a period
not exceeding three years; and censure.19
[32] The Tribunal is dealing with a matter that constitutes offences for which the health
practitioner has been convicted by a court, and therefore the Tribunal must not impose a
fine.20
[33] The Tribunal’s role is to determine the appropriate penalty, given the nature of the
conduct, to ensure that both the public interest and the integrity of the profession are
maintained. The principles for imposition of a penalty are well established. In Roberts v
PCC21 Collins J set out the relevant principles and a summary of what he said is as
follows:
(a) The first consideration requires the Tribunal to assess the penalty that most
appropriately protects the public.
(b) The Tribunal must be mindful of the fact that it plays an important role in setting
professional standards.
19 Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003, s 101(1).
20 Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003, s 101(2).
21 [2012] NZHC 3354 per Collins J at [44]-[51].

12
(c) The penalties imposed by the Tribunal may have a punitive function, although
protection of the public and setting professional standards are the most important
factors.22
(d) Where appropriate, the Tribunal must give consideration to rehabilitating health
professionals.
(e) The Tribunal should strive to ensure that any penalty it imposes is comparable to other
penalties imposed in similar circumstances.
(f) The Tribunal must assess the health professional’s behaviour against the spectrum of
the sentencing options available.
(g) The Tribunal should endeavour to impose the penalty that is the least restrictive that
can reasonably be imposed in the circumstances.
(h) The Tribunal must assess whether the penalty imposed is fair, reasonable and
proportionate in the circumstances.
[34] In A v Professional Conduct Committee,23 the Court discussed carefully the range of
sanctions available to the Tribunal, particularly cancellation and suspension. The Court
observed that four points could be expressly, and a fifth impliedly, derived from the
authorities:24
[81] First, the primary purpose of cancelling or suspending registration is to protect the
public, but that ‘inevitably imports some punitive element’. Secondly, to cancel is
more punitive than to suspend and the choice between the two turns on what is
proportionate. Thirdly, to suspend implies the conclusion that cancellation would
have been disproportionate. Fourthly, suspension is most apt where there is ‘some
condition affecting the practitioner’s fitness to practise which may or may not be
amendable to cure’. Fifthly, and perhaps only implicitly, suspension ought not to be
imposed simply to punish.
[82] Finally, the Tribunal cannot ignore the rehabilitation of the practitioner: B v B (HC
Auckland, HC 4/92, 6 April 1993) Blanchard J. Moreover, as was said in Giele v The
General Medical Council [2005] EWHC 2143, though ‘the maintenance of public
confidence…must outweigh the interests of the individual doctor,’ that is not absolute
–‘the existence of the public interest is in not ending the career of a competent doctor
will play a part.’
22 See also Singh v Director of Proceedings [2014] NZHC 2848 per Ellis J at [57], noting Collins J’s
observations in Roberts and that punishment may be an incident of the disciplinary exercise.
23 A v Professional Conduct Committee [2008] NZHC 1387 and (HC Auckland, CIV-2008-404-2927, 5
September 2008.
24 [2008] NZHC 1387 and (HC Auckland, CIV-2008-404-2927, 5 September 2008, per Keane J at [81]-
[82].

13
[35] In Katamat v Professional Conduct Committee,25 the High Court confirmed that the
primary factor in determining a penalty will be what penalty is required to protect the
public and deter similar conduct. The overall decision is ultimately one involving an
exercise of discretion.
Penalty submissions
[36] Counsel for the PCC submitted that the finding against Mr McClelland is very serious
and is at the extreme end of the spectrum as it involves a number of pornography charges
involving young children engaging in sexual acts with adult men.
[37] The PCC submitted that Mr McClelland’s name should be removed from the Register
(cancellation of registration) and that he should be censured. There is no other penalty
available to the Tribunal that would sufficiently protect the public, act as a deterrent, and
set appropriate standards for the health professions.
[38] In support of the PCC submission, counsel referred again to the Tribunal decisions of
Beardsmore26 and Lockett.27
[39] In Lockett, even though Mr Lockett had engaged in rehabilitation initiatives his
registration was cancelled.
[40] The Tribunal was not advised of Mr McClelland’s statutory release date. However, as he
was serving a prison sentence of two years or less, he would be automatically released
after serving half of his sentence (five months and one week).28 In any event, there was
no evidence before the Tribunal to indicate that Mr McClelland who is understood to have
completed his sentence and is now living in the community, has engaged in any
rehabilitation since offending other than two emails sent by him to the Nursing Council
which was then produced by the PCC.
[41] In the first email dated 19 June 2019,29 Mr McClelland stated that he was going to start
counselling and treatment “soon” and that he had undergone a “five HR assessment with
a psychologist”. The email also stated that he would “like to work in geriatrics if
possible.”
[42] In a more recent and second email dated 19 November 2019,30 Mr McClelland advised
the Nursing Council that he had commenced one-to-one counselling every fortnight with
a psychologist as well as two hour long, weekly group sessions run by WellStop. He also
indicated that he “won’t be working again.”
25 [2012] NZHC 1633 at [53].
26 243/Nur09/117P.
27 246/Nur09/119P.
28 Transcript of Evidence, p 23 lines12-22.
29 Document 4, Email form practitioners dated 19 June 2019.
30 Document 5. Email dated 19 November 2019.

14
[43] Information from the Nursing Council’s register confirmed that Mr McClelland has been
a registered nurse in New Zealand since 1996.31 He held an Annual Practising Certificate
until it expired in December 2017. He is understood to have practised in the United
Kingdom for a period of time from 2008 and he then returned to New Zealand.32 No
information was available as to whether he had been employed as a nurse in New Zealand
throughout the known period of offending.
Penalty decision
[44] The Tribunal finds that following such serious criminal convictions cancellation of
Mr McClelland’s registration is an inevitable outcome of the disciplinary process. Not
only does the Tribunal take into account the seriousness of the offending, there is also a
need to send a strong deterrent message to the profession at large that offences of this
nature involving exportation, possession and making of objectionable child publications
are abhorrent and totally unacceptable. Such offending will inevitably affect the
practitioner’s fitness to practise.
[45] Cancellation of the practitioner’s registration in this case is comparable to the penalties
imposed by the Tribunal in Beardsmore33 and Lockett34 where there were similar criminal
convictions.
[46] It is appropriate that the Tribunal makes an order for censure to express its strong
disapproval for the seriousness of the criminal offending that occurred in this case.
[47] The Tribunal considered the possibility of making formal orders under section 102 of the
Act, which provides that the Tribunal may impose one or more conditions that the person
must satisfy before the person may reapply for registration. If Mr McClelland did choose
to apply for re-registration following cancellation then having regard to the nature of the
offending and the likely importance of obtaining a psychological report, the Nursing
Council would be best placed in the light of the circumstances at the time to determine
whether it would be assisted by such a report and/or any further requirements would be
placed on Mr McClelland.
Costs
[48] The starting point is a 50% contribution to total reasonable costs of the PCC and the
Tribunal’s costs, with a discretion then to be exercised, increasing or decreasing that
amount dependent on the particular circumstances.35

32 Transcript, page 14 lines 9-25.
33 243/Nur09/117P.
34 246/Nur09/119P.
35 Cooray v Preliminary Proceedings Committee AP 23/94, 14 September 1995, Doogue J at page 9;
Vatsyayann v Professional Conduct Committee of the New Zealand Medical Council [2012] NZHC 1138,
Presley J.

15
[49] The PCC’s costs including hearing expenses and counsel were estimated as $3,361.51.36
[50] The Tribunal’s costs were estimated as $14,481.74.37
[51] Counsel for the PCC submitted that an appropriate level of contribution by
Mr McClelland would be 25% of the total costs, taking into account that whatever costs
are not awarded against Mr McClelland are picked up by the rest of the nursing
profession.
[52] It is necessary to take into account the financial circumstances of the practitioner. The
Tribunal has little knowledge of Mr McClelland’s financial circumstances other than a
credit check from a debt collection agency indicating that he had debts that he is paying
off monthly.38 He is now over 65 years and is receiving New Zealand Superannuation
from WINZ.39
[53] In reaching a decision on costs the Tribunal also takes into account that Mr McClelland
did not challenge the facts giving rise to the Charges placed before the Tribunal.
[54] The Tribunal considers that an order for a 25% contribution to the costs is a fair and
proportionate contribution to the costs of the disciplinary process; the total costs were
rounded up to $18,000, and 25% would be $4,500.
Result and Orders
[55] The Tribunal makes the following orders:
1. The Charges before the Tribunal reflect adversely on the practitioner’s fitness to
practise and are established;
2. The practitioner’s registration as a nurse will be cancelled as at the date of this
decision pursuant to s 101(1)(a) of the Act;
3. Mr McClelland is to be censured to mark the Tribunal’s condemnation of his
conduct pursuant to s 101(1)(d) of the Act;
4. There will be an order for costs of $4500 being a 25% contribution by the
practitioner to the total reasonable costs of the PCC and the Tribunal;
5. There is no application for non-publication of name and no order is made; and

SCHEDULE
PARTICULARS OF CHARGES
TAKE NOTICE that a Professional Conduct Committee (“the Committee”) appointed by the
Nursing Council of New Zealand pursuant to section 71 of the Health Practitioners
Competence Assurance Act 2003 (“the Act”) has determined, in accordance with section
80(3)(b) of the Act, that the court convictions of Milton David McClelland (Mr McClelland),
referred to the Committee pursuant to section 68(2) of the Act, should be considered by the
Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal. The Committee has reason to believe that grounds
exist entitling the Tribunal to exercise its powers under section 100 of the Act.
Charges
1. On 24 January 2019, Mr McClelland was convicted in the Palmerston North District
Court of five offences (representative) punishable by a term of imprisonment not
exceeding ten years, pursuant to section 56 of the Customs and Excise Act 1996 (as set
out in the attached Certified Copy of Entry of Criminal Record) in that:
1.1 On 18 April 2018; 24 May 2018; 9 June 2018; 22 June 2018; and 26 June 2018
he was knowingly concerned in the exportation from New Zealand of an
objectionable publication.
2. On 24 January 2019, Mr McClelland was convicted in the Palmerston North District
Court of four offences (representative) punishable by a term of imprisonment not
exceeding ten years, pursuant to section 131(A)(1) of the Films, Videos, and
Publications Classifications Act 1993 (as set out in the attached Certified Copy of
Entry of Criminal Record) in that:
2.1 On 20 September 2018 he had in his possession an objectionable publication
knowing or having reasonable cause to believe the publication was
objectionable namely five electronic image files located on an optical disc
labelled ‘Mypix’ ;
2.2 On 20 September 2018 without lawful authority or excuse he had in his
possession an objectionable publication knowing or having reasonable cause
to believe the publication was objectionable namely five electronic image files
located on an optical disc labelled ‘Mypix 2’;

18
2.3 On 20 September 2018 without lawful authority or excuse he had in his
possession an objectionable publication knowing or having reasonable cause
to believe the publication was objectionable namely four electronic image files
located on Vodafone VFD 200 mobile phone; and
2.4 On 20 September 2018 without lawful authority or excuse he had in his
possession an objectionable publication knowing or having reasonable cause
to believe the publication was objectionable namely six electronic image files
located on Vodafone VFD 511 mobile phone.
3. On 24 January 2019, Mr McClelland was convicted in the Palmerston North District
Court of one offence (representative) punishable by a term of imprisonment not
exceeding 14 years, pursuant to section 124(1) of the Films, Videos, and Publications
Classifications Act 1993 (as set out in the attached Certified Copy of Entry of
Criminal Record) in that:
3.1 Between 31 July 2018 and 28 August 2018 made an objectionable publication,
knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the publication was
objectionable, namely five video files located on a Vodafone VFD511 mobile
phone.
These convictions separately and cumulatively reflect adversely on Mr McClelland’s fitness
to practise pursuant to section 100(1)(c) of the Act.
